## Current Code Workflow (from code analyzer)
# Model Overview (for Diagnosis)

The supplied code contains the diagnosis module, not the GRU4Rec implementation. Diagnosis examines item embeddings and per-position sequence features exposed through ModelView. `log2feats(sequence)` supplies these features; `predict_score(features, items)` produces candidate logits. The model’s representation computation cannot be verified here. Final inference on left-padded histories must select the final nonpadding position; these probes instead score all positions with nonzero positive targets.

# Diagnosis Inputs & Hooks

`DiagnosisProbe(view, device)` stores the view and accesses `item_emb`, `user_train`, `meta_data`, and `review_data`; histories and review data are stored but unused. The underlying module is available as `view.model`.

The loader yields `(None, sequence, positive, negative)` with tensors shaped `B × L`. The probe calls `eval()` and scores up to ten batches without gradients. Paired candidate IDs have shape `B × L × 2`.

# Probes & Metrics

- **`embedding_collapse_score`**: Samples at most 2,048 real-item embeddings with seed 42, excluding padding and reserved tokens. It normalizes vectors, averages off-diagonal cosine similarities, and maps the result using `(mean + 1)/2`. Higher values indicate directional alignment; approximately 0.5 represents near-zero average cosine, not necessarily collapse.
- **`pos_neg_margin_mean` / `pos_neg_margin_p10`**: Mean and tenth percentile of positive-minus-negative logits over nonzero positive targets. Higher values suggest stronger separation.
- **`pos_neg_neg_beats_pos_rate`**: Fraction of margins below zero; lower is better.
- **`pos_neg_small_margin_rate`**: Fraction below 0.5; lower indicates fewer weakly separated pairs.
- **`pos_neg_margin_category_breakdown`**: Counts low-margin and wrong-ranking positions and lists the top 20 metadata categories separately for positive and negative items.

# Perturbation & Tests

No sequence shuffling, masking, ablation, or sensitivity perturbation is performed. Random embedding subsampling estimates geometric alignment; supplied positive/negative pairs test training-position discrimination.

# MODEL_DIAGNOSIS Schema & Limitations

`run_full_diagnosis` returns `metrics` and `metric_definitions`. `diagnosis_interpreter_prompt` embeds both into instructions requesting a JSON interpretation with `status`, `core_findings`, `key_implications`, and `evidence`.

These probes do not measure validation HR@10, full-catalog recommendation diversity, temporal sensitivity, or generalization. Margins depend on logit scale and sampled negatives. Category metadata is unavailable in this task, so category lists should remain empty. Empty margin samples return zeros, which must not be mistaken for healthy measurements.

The closest match is [Does It Look Sequential? (RecSys 2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.12008), which evaluates sequence shuffling across 15 datasets. Its [official implementation](https://github.com/Antondfger/Does-It-Look-Sequential) keeps trained GRU4Rec models fixed and compares original versus shuffled inference histories using HR@10, NDCG@10 and recommendation-list Jaccard@10. Effects vary sharply: reported GRU4Rec HR@10 changes include −25% on Beauty, −63% on MovieLens-20M and −7% on Yelp. This supports measuring both target accuracy and recommendation stability; weak accuracy changes alone do not establish that predictions are unchanged.

Recency is a related but distinct question. [RSS (2025)](https://eprints.gla.ac.uk/299238/) motivates recency-aware training samples, while [DyS4Rec (2025)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0893608025000139) addresses historical interactions irrelevant to next-interaction intent. Suggested diagnostic extension: on training-history next-item holdouts, compare equal-sized recent versus older deletions, progressively retain shorter recent suffixes, and shuffle either the whole history or only the prefix while preserving the last item. Keep the trained checkpoint, targets and candidate sets fixed; report paired target-rank changes, HR@10 changes, top-10 Jaccard and final-state cosine distance, with user-level uncertainty. Repack perturbed histories with left padding and read the final nonpadding position. Larger effects from recent deletions indicate recency sensitivity; prefix-shuffle effects with the last item fixed suggest dependence beyond the latest interaction. These are proposed sensitivity probes, not direct measurements of latent intent or causal proof of stale preferences.

Applied here, each proposed rejection reason should include a supporting history event or title/description span, its timestamp where relevant, and a supported/contradicted/insufficient-evidence label. These papers validate grounding methods, not the ability to recover actual rejection reasons from implicit interactions.

Recommended adaptation: distinguish observable repetition or explicit specification conflicts from unknown personal fit. Similar titles can indicate content overlap, but do not establish ownership, unwanted redundancy, device ownership, mood, or current intent. Recent interactions provide temporal context rather than proof of a present need. Annotate item facts separately from user-fit claims; abstain when the latter lack evidence. Treat these as proposed controls requiring local validation. Without explicit user rejection feedback, the resulting labels measure evidence-supported failure hypotheses, not confirmed reasons for rejection.

            Zero padding embeddings do not make GRU padding steps inert. `Embedding(padding_idx=0)` initializes a fixed zero padding vector, but GRU gates still apply recurrent transformations and biases at every timestep. Consequently, leading zeros can change the hidden state before the first real item, making identical histories behave differently with different padding lengths. This follows from the documented [GRU equations](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/main/generated/torch.nn.GRU.html) and [embedding behavior](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.nn.Embedding).

For computation equivalent to unpadded histories, compact each left-padded history into a valid prefix, right-pad for batching, then use `pack_padded_sequence(..., batch_first=True, enforce_sorted=False)`. Packing uses the supplied lengths to retain prefixes; directly packing left-padded tensors would retain padding and truncate real items. Alternatively, explicitly preserve every recurrent layer’s previous hidden state at padding positions. Masking only the final outputs cannot undo earlier recurrent updates. See [packing documentation](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/main/generated/torch.nn.utils.rnn.pack_padded_sequence.html).

Suggested verification: in evaluation mode with identical weights and initial states, compare each history processed alone without padding against packed-batch and explicitly masked execution. Compare final features and candidate scores with numerical tolerances, and repeat with different leading-padding lengths and batch companions. Handle empty histories separately. For original left-padded layouts, read the final nonpadding position—normally the last column—not `length-1`; that index applies only after compaction into a valid prefix.

“Does It Look Sequential?” (RecSys 2024) evaluates GRU4Rec and SASRec by shuffling inference histories while keeping holdout targets fixed, using the same trained checkpoint. It measures HR@10/NDCG@10 degradation and top-10 Jaccard overlap; several datasets show weak sensitivity. Crucially, excluding the holdout target from shuffling does **not** preserve the latest input interaction. Its shuffle therefore combines disruption of the last-item signal with disruption of earlier order, and cannot isolate longer-context dependence. [Paper](https://arxiv.org/html/2408.12008v1)

For the proposed GRU4Rec diagnosis, use paired validation-only controls on the same checkpoint: original history; last-item-only input; shuffle earlier interactions while fixing the last input item; and delete equal numbers of recent versus oldest interactions while preserving that last item in both conditions. Repack and left-pad consistently, retaining identical users, targets and candidate sets. These are proposed diagnostic extensions, not the paper’s reported protocol. A drop under last-preserving shuffling indicates sensitivity to earlier order; a larger drop from recent-context deletion than oldest deletion suggests reliance on nearby context beyond the last item. Last-item-only similarity instead suggests that most predictive value comes from the latest interaction, although truncation also changes the input distribution. Complement HR@10 changes with recommendation-list overlap: accuracy can remain stable while recommendations change. The broader distinction between last-item evidence, accumulated earlier-item evidence and joint sequence modelling is articulated in [Spotify’s benchmark analysis](https://research.atspotify.com/2026/10/do-sequential-recommendation-benchmarks-require-higher-order-sequence-modelling).

Sampled ranking metrics measure performance against the sampled candidates; they need not preserve full-catalog model rankings, even in expectation ([Krichene & Rendle](https://research.google/pubs/on-sampled-metrics-for-item-recommendation/)). For paired perturbation diagnostics, keep each user’s target and candidate set identical before/after perturbation. Adapting [paired bootstrap resampling](https://aclanthology.org/W04-3250/), resample users with replacement while retaining their paired outcomes; cluster multiple observations from the same user. For this four-category benchmark, resample users within each category and recompute the equal-weight macro-average difference. Interpretation: uncertainty conditional on the fitted models and realized candidate sets; excludes retraining variability and negative-sampling variability. Bootstrap replicates neither retrain nor combine predictors.

Sequence shuffling has been used to probe sequential structure ([Does It Look Sequential?](https://publications.hse.ru/en/chapters/984043670)). For a fixed model, however, inference-time perturbation measures sensitivity to changed inputs, potentially outside its training distribution; a performance drop alone does not establish causal dependence on sequence order. Distinguish target-item exposure elsewhere in training, legitimate repeated consumption, and exposure to the exact evaluated user–target interaction. The last makes the probe partly an in-sample recall/memorization diagnostic, rather than evidence of unseen-interaction generalization; item exposure alone does not establish leakage. Report exposure status, paired effect sizes and confidence intervals, and perturbation details. Preserve item multiplicities, sequence length, padding and targets when isolating order effects; separate order changes from deletions or recency changes. These are methodological implications for the proposed diagnostic, not findings about the current models.
